questions.stem: A colleague proposes one integer variable per project, its start year from 2027 to 2034, instead of one binary per project and year. What does that cost the model?

options.text: Each year's spend becomes a fraction of the start year, so the model needs more constraints
options.says: Spend does not scale with the year number; it depends on which year the start is, which is the nonlinearity.

options.text: Each year's spend becomes a nonlinear function of the start year, so the model is no longer a MILP
options.says: Right: with binaries, NPV and spend by year are sums of data times variables; with one integer they depend on it nonlinearly.

options.text: Nothing, since an integer start year carries the same information as the binaries
options.says: The information is the same, but the expressions over it stop being linear.

options.text: Nothing, since each year's NPV can still be read off the integer as a sum
options.says: With one integer start year, NPV and spend depend on it nonlinearly; only the binaries make them sums.

origin.section: One Binary per Project and Start Year Turns "When" Into "Whether"

questions.stem: A test of a new timing model finds project P17 in the solution twice, starting in 2028 and in 2030, and the reported NPV counts both. Which row is missing?

options.text: The sum of P17's start variables is at least one, so it starts at least once
options.says: That forces P17 to start, which is the must-do rule; it does not stop a second start.

options.text: The budget row of 2030, since the second start overspends that year
options.says: The second start may fit the budget; the defect is that a project can start twice at all.

options.text: The sum of P17's start variables is at most one, so it starts at most once
options.says: Right: without that row, nothing stops two start variables of one project from both being 1.

options.text: The window row of P17, since 2030 is outside its window
options.says: A window is enforced by not creating variables; the variable for 2030 existed, so 2030 was in the window.

origin.section: A Project Starts at Most Once, and a Must-Do Starts Exactly Once

questions.stem: A project with a three-year cost profile may start from 2029 to 2033, and the plan's horizon ends in 2034. Which start variables should the model create?

options.text: Starts in 2029 to 2032, since a 2033 start would still be spending after 2034
options.says: Right: a start in t spends through t + 2, so 2032 is the last start that finishes inside the horizon.

options.text: Starts in 2029 to 2033, since the planners allowed every year in the window
options.says: A 2033 start spends in 2035, outside the plan, so the model would fund work it never pays for.

options.text: Starts in 2027 to 2034, since the solver discards years that break the window
options.says: Nothing would discard them unless you add rows; leaving them out is the window.

options.text: Starts in 2029 to 2034, since the horizon ends in 2034
options.says: The horizon bounds the spending, not the start; a late start spends past it.

origin.section: A Timing Window Is Enforced by the Variables You Never Create
